title: Dynamic Hotspot Migration and Self-Induced Resonances in Ultrafast Laser-Irradiated Silicon Thin Films
authors: George D. Tsibidis, Yi Wang, Emmanuel Stratakis
abstract: The spatial distribution of energy in silicon thin films under femtosecond laser irradiation is demonstrated to be influenced by the interaction between carrier-induced refractive index modulation and self-induced Fabry-Pérot resonances. We resolve three characteristic excitation regions such as interface-localized, binodal and multi-nodal regimes considering the analysis of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) configurations across thicknesses of 100, 230, and 350 nm. We report a nonlinear hotspot migration effect where the transient reduction of the refractive index stretches the internal standing wave, translating intensity antinodes toward the film volume during the pulse. Numerical results demonstrate that at higher fluences, plasma-induced extinction suppresses internal reflections, triggering a transition from resonance-mediated absorption to plasma shielding. These findings establish a physical basis for depth-resolved modification in laser nanomanufacturing, providing a dual-capacity for simultaneous surface patterning and depth-resolved subsurface modification with direct applications in laser-assisted interfacial separation and 3D integrated photonic fabrication.
summary: This work models how ultrafast laser pulses interact with silicon thin films, showing that energy deposition is governed by dynamic resonances influenced by free carrier generation. By controlling the laser fluence, researchers can switch the energy deposition from deep subsurface structuring to surface-only modification, enabling advanced, depth-controlled nanomanufacturing techniques.
main_problem: The study investigates how the spatial energy distribution in silicon thin films changes when irradiated by ultrafast lasers, focusing on the interplay between carrier-induced refractive index changes and self-induced Fabry-Pérot resonances.
main_result: The energy deposition can be dynamically controlled by modulating the laser fluence, allowing a transition between subsurface resonant structuring and surface-limited plasma shielding.
method: The research employs self-consistent dynamic multireflection theory, coupling carrier excitation, the two-temperature model, and dynamic electromagnetic simulations.
model_or_system: The system involves Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) architectures with thicknesses ranging from 100 nm to 350 nm, irradiated by femtosecond laser pulses.
key_observables: Energy deposition profile (intensity distribution), carrier density ($N_e$), refractive index ($n_{Si}$), and lattice temperature.
important_parameters: Laser fluence ($0.4$ and $0.7$ J/cm$^2$), film thickness ($100, 230, 350$ nm), and carrier-induced refractive index collapse.
main_assumptions: The model assumes films are much smaller than the laser spot radius, allowing for 1D modeling along the propagation axis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spatio-temporal intensity and carrier density distributions for various thicknesses and fluences, showing the evolution of hotspots and the transition between different energy localization regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by analyzing different film thicknesses (interface-localized, binodal, multi-nodal) under varying fluences, demonstrating the dynamic hotspot migration effect, and concluding with the physical basis for depth-resolved laser nanomanufacturing.
why_interesting: The dynamic coupling between carrier dynamics and the optical response (refractive index modulation) provides a rich, non-equilibrium system analogous to open quantum systems where the environment (plasma) actively modifies the system's Hamiltonian (optical properties).
